name: Software engineering: mutation-adequate test generation for CPython's statistics
description: Generate at most 30 test calls for statistics (averages, medians, quantiles, spread, correlation, regression and NormalDist) that distinguish as many of its 583 first-order mutants as possible from the original module. A mutant is killed when some test's result or exception type differs; the score is the fraction killed.

sources.locator: Fraser and Zeller (TSE 2012): generating unit tests and oracles that kill mutants.
DeMillo and Offutt (TSE 1991): constraint-based generation of test data that kills mutants.
Lukasczyk, Kroiss and Fraser (EMSE 2023): automated unit test generation for Python (Pynguin), assessed by coverage and mutation score.
Papadakis, Jia, Harman and Le Traon (ICSE 2015): trivial compiler equivalence for removing equivalent mutants.
CPython 3.12.14 source release (PSF licence): the mutated modules.

requirements.datasets: CPython 3.12.14 source release (PSF licence), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py.

evaluation.benchmark: Software engineering: mutation-adequate test generation for CPython's statistics
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: generate_tests(subject) -> list of tests. subject = {'subject': str, 'files': {path: source} (CPython 3.12.14), 'target': path of the mutated module, 'api': {call: [argument kinds]}, 'mutants': [{'unit', 'operator', 'line', 'start', 'end', 'replacement'}, ...], 'max_tests': 30}. A test is {'call': name, 'args': [values]}. Argument kinds: 'str' (at most 500 characters), 'int' (|n| <= 10000), 'opt_int' (such an int or None), 'bool', 'float' (finite, |x| <= 1e6), 'fraction' (a str of at most 30 characters for Fraction(), with an exponent of at most two digits), 'spec' (a format spec of at most 12 characters without runs of four digits), 'number' (a 'fraction' str, an int with |n| <= 1000 or a float), 'numbers' (a list of at most 40 values, each a 'fraction' str, an int with |n| <= 10000 or a float with |x| <= 1e6), 'pairs' (at most 20 [str, str] pairs of at most 100 characters each), {'options': {keyword: kind}} (keyword arguments), {'strings': n} (exactly n strings), {'choice': [allowed values]}. Calls: textwrap: wrap/fill/shorten(text, width, options) -> textwrap.<call>(text, width, **options), dedent(text), indent(text, prefix); urllib.parse: each call is the function of that name with the arguments in order (urlparse/urlsplit(url, scheme, allow_fragments), urljoin(base, url, allow_fragments), parse_qs/parse_qsl(qs, keep_blank_values, strict_parsing, max_num_fields, separator), quote/quote_plus(string, safe)), urlunparse/urlunsplit get the strings as a tuple, urlencode(pairs, doseq, safe) passes the pairs as tuples; fractions: parse(s) -> Fraction(s), make(n, d) -> Fraction(n, d), from_float(x), binary(a, op, b) applies the operator (or divmod, max) to a and b with str operands converted by Fraction, limit_denominator(s, m), round(s, ndigits) (round(Fraction(s)) when ndigits is None), format(s, spec) -> format(Fraction(s), spec), method(s, name) -> getattr(Fraction(s), name)(); statistics (str values become Fraction): summary(name, data) -> statistics.<name>(data), median_grouped(data, interval), quantiles(data, n, method), weighted(name, data, weights) -> fmean or harmonic_mean with weights, spread_given_center(name, data, c) -> variance/pvariance/stdev/pstdev(data, c), bivariate(name, x, y) -> covariance, correlation (linear or ranked) or linear_regression (proportional or not), normal(mu, sigma, method, x) -> NormalDist(mu, sigma).method(x) (quantiles(int(x)) for 1 <= x <= 1000, overlap(NormalDist(x, 1.0))), from_samples(data). A mutant is the target file with lines start..end replaced by 'replacement'; it is killed when some test's outcome differs from the original module's outcome, where the outcome is a hash of the repr of the result (generators consumed, at most 10,001 items) or the type name of the raised exception. A call is cut off, with the outcome 'timeout', when it exceeds 50,000 steps or its CPU-time limit. A step is a function entry or a loop iteration inside a function of the given files, so the count does not depend on the machine (the largest call the argument bounds allow needs about 10,000 steps). The CPU-time limit is 0.2 s on the original module and 0.2 s plus ten times the original's own CPU time on a mutant; it only matters for calls that spend long inside C code or whose iterations grow ever more expensive. Tests that time out on the original are ignored. Score: killed mutants / all mutants, maximised (equivalent mutants make 1.0 unreachable); the whole mutation analysis may take at most 240 s of CPU time, otherwise the evaluation is invalid. generate_tests() runs in a sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 60 s CPU, 2 GB) and may load the files and mutants itself; it should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks). Invalid tests make the evaluation invalid.

limitations: Mutants come from this evaluator's operator set (MutPy- and mutmut-style replacements inside function bodies); scores are not comparable with other mutation tools.
Non-compiling, duplicate and trivially compiler-equivalent mutants are removed, but other equivalent mutants remain, so 1.0 is unreachable and the number of killable mutants is unknown.
Oracles are regression oracles: a test kills a mutant when the hash of the result's repr or the exception type differs from the original's, which also counts differences a specification might allow.

Reference computed with this evaluator (Linux x86-64, CPython 3.12): the seed's generate_tests with max_tests = 2000, i.e. 2,000 random calls, kills 345 of the 583 mutants (59.2%); the 30-test budget is this dataset's choice.
The candidate sees the mutants and may run them, so the task measures test generation and selection against known mutants, not generalisation to unseen faults.
The module's optional C accelerator for NormalDist.inv_cdf (_statistics) is disabled by a one-line patch so that its Python implementation is the one mutated and tested.

Step counting makes the verdict on loops independent of the machine, but CPU-time limits remain as a safety net: a test whose call on the original module needs about 0.2 s of CPU time (very large powers, tab expansion to megabytes or long exact-fraction computations: 9,999 quantiles of 40 fractions need 0.06 s on the machine used for this record) is used or ignored depending on the machine.

Outcomes are compared exactly, so a result that depends on the last digits of the C math library can differ between platforms: the seed kills 152 of the 583 mutants on Linux x86-64 with glibc and 150 on macOS arm64. The two extra kills are mutants of NormalDist.cdf (1.0 + erf(...) changed to 1.0 - erf(...) and to 2.0 + erf(...)), which leave NormalDist.overlap unchanged mathematically and change its floating-point result in the 15th significant digit only where erf rounds differently.

state_of_the_art.statement: No published value exists for this mutant set. As a reference, the seed's generate_tests with max_tests = 2000 (2,000 random calls) kills 345 of the 583 mutants (59.2%) (computed with this evaluator on Linux x86-64).

sources.title: Mutation-Driven Generation of Unit Tests and Oracles

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Automated unit test generation with strong oracles: produce a small set of tests that detects as many seeded faults (mutants) of a module as possible.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Mutation score is the standard measure of a test suite's fault-detection ability; generating tests that kill mutants automates oracle and input design for unit testing.
